title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
description: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Ku
body: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law"."The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran."If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
description: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kreml
body: The meeting hasn't even happened yet. But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin. Whatever the outcome.Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed."We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."But what of those who are not at the table?Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe."We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

schema.headline: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin

title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
description: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.
body: Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president. After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin and Trump have not yet held a substantive meeting, and merely greeted each other on Wednesday.Peskov also said that "no more than an hour" had been allocated for Thursday's trilateral talks between Putin, Trump and Xi.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.It is unclear whether China would want this issue to be on the agenda in Shenzhen, with Beijing talking more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough. Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special". In Shenzhen, a red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

schema.headline: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China

title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz outclasses Daniil Medvedev despite injury concern
description: Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to all but confirm his progress at the AT
body: Carlos Alcaraz continued his sensational late-season form as he outclassed world number five Daniil Medvedev to all but confirm his progress at the ATP Finals.But the 23-year-old Spaniard later said he had felt "a little problem" with his hamstring.Alcaraz produced another sparkling display to control the contest throughout, despite ending the match with heavy strapping on his upper-left leg.The issue did not disrupt the world number three, who led by a set and a break when he received treatment on the area, as he cruised to a 6-2 6-4 win in just 72 minutes."Right now I'm just feeling OK," Alcaraz said."We will see with my team and physio, but I think the rest of today and tomorrow are really going to be important days ahead of me."It was an 11th consecutive victory for the seven-time major winner, following back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters.Alcaraz will qualify for the semi-finals before his last group match against Flavio Cobolli on Friday if Frances Tiafoe wins a set against the Italian later on Wednesday.Asked what pleased him most about his performance, Alcaraz replied: "Everything"."We could see in [Medvedev's] first match that he was serving very well. I returned really well, really aggressively, and really deep," he added."I think I just hit the ball in a sweet spot every time. I'm really happy about it."Given the outstanding levels at which he is currently operating, it is easy to forget that Alcaraz spent four months out of action in the middle of the season.The former world number one's rapid return from that wrist injury to his scintillating best has been astonishing.Alcaraz has won three titles and lost just twice in 24 matches since making his return at the US Open in August, when his lack of match fitness appeared to catch up with him in a four-and-a-half hour epic against Ben Shelton.Just 10 weeks on, he delivered one of the best indoor performances of his career in sweeping past 2020 champion Medvedev. That came two days after he began his latest bid for a first ATP Finals title with a statement victory over Tiafoe - and later warned his rivals he has never felt better at this stage of the season.Medvedev beat home hope Cobolli in straight sets in his opening match for his first win against a top-10 opponent since defeating Alcaraz at Indian Wells in March.The Russian was no match for the Australian Open champion on this occasion, however.A dominant seven-game streak ultimately decided the match, as Alcaraz ran away with the first set and then broke immediately in the second to take firm control.The second seed did not face a single break point as he outmanoeuvred Medvedev, firing 16 winners and committing just 13 unforced errors.It was a display which scored 9.5 out of 10 on the ATP's performance rating, which combines several statistics to measure a player's overall game, following a 9.6 in his opener.That was despite Alcaraz playing the final seven games with the issue in his hamstring, which he will now work to overcome in the next 48 hours.

schema.headline: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz outclasses Daniil Medvedev despite injury concern

title: Rassie Erasmus: How South Africa's maverick coach divides rugby
description: Alternative views are available.While Rassie Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, in his homeland they rushed to his defence."Rassie was just a
body: Alternative views are available.While Rassie Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, in his homeland they rushed to his defence."Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' six-match ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his Springboks side."But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance?"Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me they [officials] are untouchable," he said.Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.Despite slurring the officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.It is not surprising.His feats with the team are astonishing.South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.He arrived off the back of a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented three-peat. And few would bet against them achieving it.Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match. He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.Legally, he is across every possible loophole.There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off. Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town."He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social."I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards."He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions."Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement."Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.Some also see instinctive honesty rather than premeditated ploy in his public speaking."He also has almost no filters, so he will speak his mind without fully appreciating the consequences of what he has done," his biographer David O'Sullivan told BBC Sport in 2023.Whatever the motivation, the consequences keep coming - for Erasmus, but also the rest of world rugby.Referees Nic Berry and Wayne Barnes, previous targets of Erasmus' criticism, have detailed the effects it had on them.Berry described "a character assassination" that caused "immeasurable damage". He has not refereed a South Africa game in the five years since.Barnes' wife and children were threatened over social media.South Africa's latest appeal to their supporters not to abuse officials, external may be too late for referee Andrea Piardi and his television match official Matteo Liperini, who oversaw France's win on Friday.There is a wider question too.For a complex sport, the image of a world champion coach publicly criticising officials does not little to dispel a wavering viewer's assumption that it is too intricate and confusing to justify their attention.South Africa will always line up alongside their rebel chief.But the patience of the rest of the rugby world with Erasmus' antics is wearing ever thinner.

schema.headline: Rassie Erasmus: How South Africa's maverick coach divides rugby

title: Brain cancer patients at UHCW demand public inquiry into chemotherapy scandal
description: Image caption, Becky Jones who had 11 years of chemotherapy for a cancer she did not have said treatment was "handed out like sweets"ByDavid Lumbin Co
body: Image caption, Becky Jones who had 11 years of chemotherapy for a cancer she did not have said treatment was "handed out like sweets"ByDavid Lumbin CoventryShehnaz Khan and Oprah FlashWest MidlandsUpdated 3 hours agoBrain cancer patients who were given years of unnecessary chemotherapy are calling for a public inquiry, after a review found people were severely harmed under an NHS trust's care.Some were misdiagnosed while others were told if they stopped temozolomide (TMZ) treatment they would die, despite this not being true.The Royal College of Physicians (RCP) investigated 20 cases at University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust.The drug is typically meant to be taken for six months but in one case a patient of Prof Ian Brown was given more than 100 cycles of chemotherapy over a period of 13 years. They later developed leukaemia as a side-effect of too much chemotherapy.Becky Jones, who had 11 years of the treatment for a cancer she did not have, has told the BBC she was "absolutely disgusted" that "chemotherapy was dished out like it was sweets".Image source, UHCWImage caption, University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust has apologised"I have two young children and to think once upon a time I might not have been there for their future kills me every day and it's all down to one person," the 35-year-old added.She is one of more than 40 patients taking legal action against the NHS Trust. The mum-of-two was 21 when she was told she had a grade 4 glioblastoma and six to 12 months to live.After more than 100 cycles of chemotherapy it was found she had never had a brain tumour and that her imaging was consistent with tumefactive demyelination, a less serious lesion.She said of the report: "The findings are worse than I ever expected them to be."A national inquiry needs to happen and things need to be tightened up so it can't happen to anyone else."I don't think I'll ever find closure until the trust accept what they have done wrong and are held accountable. I would like answers."The review, released on Wednesday, was commissioned by the trust following the retirement of one of its doctors.Brown, referred to as Dr Y in the RCP's report, did not take part in the review and refused to comment when approached by the BBC at his home.University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust has apologised for "failures" within its neuro-oncology service under the care of the retired clinical oncologist.Chief executive Professor Andy Hardy and trust chair Sue Noyes said in a statement: "This is far below the standards our patients deserve and that we expect. We let you down, and for that we offer our sincere apologies."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Prof Ian Brown, who retired in 2024, is referred to as Dr Y in the reviewBrown was employed there from 1996 to 2024 and concerns over his practice were raised by colleagues when his patients were handed over upon his retirement in December 2023.Medics found people on long-term repeated cycles of TMZ, against standard practice and national guidelines.Some patients had also been left on treatment despite their cancer progressing, when moving to the best supportive care for their symptoms would have been a better choice.More than 80 treatedTMZ, a chemotherapy drug that is sometimes used for glioblastoma and astrocytoma brain tumours, should usually be taken post radiotherapy for six cycles, usually over six months, but some patients have told the BBC they received it for many years.The review warned there may be many more affected patients, with 83 receiving extended TMZ treatment between 2017 and 2023.Overall, the RCP examined 20 cases of care under Brown, though the number of patients affected is higher - including those who have since died.Working to strict definitions of harm, the review team concluded six patients had suffered severe harm, five moderate harm and eight low levels of harm. In the final case, the review team could not reach a judgement on moderate or severe harm.Among other recommendations, the RCP said that any wider review of patients who received the treatment and have since died should be discussed with the Department of Health and Social Care."There is a large cohort of deceased patients who have received this non-standard chemotherapy regime, who may potentially have come to harm," the report said. "To review every patient would be a significant and costly undertaking. The Trust should determine whether such a step is appropriate, and if so, discuss with the DHSC and/or NHS England how such a review would proceed."Image caption, After 10 years of treatment, Mark Poulton found out he had been wrongly diagnosedFather-of-three Mark Poulton, from Redditch, Worcestershire, said he had been left in "constant pain" with spells of depression after undergoing chemotherapy for a decade, only to discover two years ago that he had been misdiagnosed.The 54-year-old told the BBC: "I feel angry that I've gone through 10 years of TMZ that I probably shouldn't have done and the report backs that."You get a cancer diagnosis of any sort and you feel you will collapse, then you go to a hospital and you're in the right place, you feel safe, only to find out 10 to 12 years later that you were abused by the system that failed me and the other patients involved."More needs to be done, it can't end here with this review. We need action so it doesn't happen again."In 2014 he was told he had oligodendroglioma, an aggressive brain tumour, but found out in 2024 that he actually had astrocytoma, a different type of cancer.'Significant toxicity'The review also highlighted patients who were exposed to a "significant lifetime risk" of developing secondary cancers and other health problems after several years of non-standard chemotherapy.One, who received the drug for 10 years, experienced "significant toxicity", including ongoing fatigue, nausea and a "severe episode" of ophthalmic shingles and galactorrhoea caused by a drug prescribed to treat chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.The review also referred to a Mr N, who the BBC understands to be clinical nurse specialist Ian Edwards.Some patients were advised implicitly and explicitly that stopping treatment would be harmful, the review said.There was also evidence in some cases of patients being given misleading information.The review team heard in interviews that a small number of patients had requested discontinuation of their treatment, which Edwards then discussed with Brown and acted upon, however no evidence of this was seen in the cases reviewed."In one case when the patient questioned their treatment, they were told by Mr N  (Edwards) that Dr Y (Brown) was 'legally bound' to continue it," they added.Edwards has also since retired from the trust, UHCW confirmed, adding it had made a formal regulatory referral to the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) regulator.Image caption, Becky Addison of law firm Brabners said the report was "thorough" but patients still need answersLegal firm Brabners, which represents more than 40 patients and is calling for an independent public inquiry, said cases had been referred to the police but no action had yet been taken.Becky Addison, from the firm, said: "Now is the opportunity that everyone needs to sit up and look at how important this is for patients that they get the answers that they deserve. "They've had their lives taken away from them in unimaginable ways and all that they need at the moment is answers, transparency and accountability and that will come by way of a statutory public inquiry."All living patients receiving TMZ at the trust have already had their care reviewed again internally to ensure it aligned with expected standards, the UHCW trust has said.A "comprehensive independent external clinical review process" will also evaluate all living patients who received over 12 cycles of TMZ under Brown.The trust added: "We have initiated discussions with the NHS England regional director of patient safety to establish clear requirements and methodology for reviewing the cohort of deceased patients who received non-standard chemotherapy regime."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Coventry & Warwickshire

schema.headline: Brain cancer patients at UHCW demand public inquiry into chemotherapy scandal

title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House
description: Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black law
body: Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will hold a majority of the seats. As of Wednesday, Democrats will have at least 257 seats in the House next year, with seven races still uncalled.His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the partnership of a Democrat-controlled Senate.Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote, Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change."While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but he has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like. That could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms. Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel. Many of the incoming liberal Democrats, and members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.Jeffries will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.

schema.headline: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House

title: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page reveals 'awful' comments from male actor
description: Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.The Swansea-born actress, 48, t
body: Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene."He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers. Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something"."And it was just, like, really inappropriate, awful stuff."

schema.headline: I'm a Celeb: Joanna Page reveals 'awful' comments from male actor

title: George thought his funeral was paid for – but now his wife will get nothing when he dies
description: Image caption, George Davies says he feels resentful towards the insurance companiesByEmma Clifford BellBBC ScotlandUpdated 18 November 2026 06:07 GMT
body: Image caption, George Davies says he feels resentful towards the insurance companiesByEmma Clifford BellBBC ScotlandUpdated 18 November 2026 06:07 GMTFor 17 years, George Davies made payments to an insurance company to cover the cost of his funeral.The 82-year-old, who has stage 4 cancer, thought he had prepared and provided for his wife Marion.But now he isn't entitled to a penny.George took the policy out through his local credit union, but it was cancelled after the company backing the product pulled out of the UK.Credit unions say the closure of the plan has left thousands of people like George in limbo, with many unable to arrange an affordable alternative because they are elderly or unwell.A coalition of 17 credit unions across Scotland and the north of England is calling for those affected to receive fair compensation.'I worry about it all the time'George, from Bellshill in North Lanarkshire, is currently undergoing palliative care after being diagnosed with oesophageal cancer in 2023.He says he can't sleep at night because of worrying about how his wife of 50 years will cope when he's gone."I needed something to leave to Marion so that she didn't have to worry about funeral expenses," he says."The only consolation is that when I die, I stop worrying about it. I just worry about it all the time."George had been paying into a policy called the Family Protection Plan (FPP), which he took out through Mosshill Credit Union.He initially thought it was "excellent", promising a cash lump sum on death to policy holders and up to five named family members.But as his health deteriorates, George says he feels resentful towards the insurance companies involved."How can these people do these things?" he asks. "I'm going to need this money sooner than later."Image caption, George said he had not wanted his wife Marion to worry about funeral expensesThe FFP was a renewable life insurance product which did not build up a cash value over time and could be cancelled with 30 days' notice.It closed in November 2025, leaving about 5,000 people across the UK without cover.The Family Protection Plan was first offered in 1999 and closed to new business in 2009, with cover continuing for those already on the scheme.Although the money could be used for any purpose, BBC Scotland News understands that it was initially advertised to help cover the cost of funerals.An early leaflet, provided to us by the credit unions, says the FPP could be used for "any of the costs associated with the funeral" – including the wake and travel expenses for relatives.It was sold exclusively through credit unions to their members.Credit unions are not-for-profit financial institutions where members pool their savings to lend to one another. They are often community-based and offer an alternative to traditional banking.'Stand up and be accountable'FPP was offered by insurance broker CMutual, which was formerly known as CUNA Mutual Group.The underwriters on the policy changed over the years, with Maiden Life covering the plan between 2022 and 2025.Maiden Life announced it would leave the UK market in 2024 and gave notice of termination.CMutual was unable to find another suitable insurer and the plan closed in November 2025.The coalition of credit unions group says it represents about 1,500 people who have been affected by the closure. Some have paid premiums for up to 25 years.Julie Reddin is the chief executive of Mosshill credit union and co-chairs the coalition, which is campaigning for members to receive a fair pay out.She says it is a "scandal" that so many people have lost out on what they regarded as funeral cover."We would just like the people that have made money out of the policies to actually stand up and be accountable and not step back and say no that wasn't us," she says."It may not have been illegal what they did, but it was immoral."Image caption, Julie Reddin says legislation needs to be changedCredit unions in the coalition have agreed to help with the cost of funerals for affected members as a goodwill gesture as they feel a level of responsibility.At the time the FPP closed, Julie's branch had 139 members with the policy. She says many are now nearing the end of their life – like George."We've had 11 people pass away since the policy closed at a cost of £58,000 to our credit union," she says.Julie estimates it would cost Mosshill Credit Union £1.3m to cover all policies."If we had to pay that out straight away, the credit union would go into liquidation. We just don't have that type of money to pay out," she said.Julie says the Financial Conduct Authority should have stepped in sooner and wants financial redress for the most vulnerable customers to be split between credit unions, CMutual and Maiden Life."Legislation needs to be changed - this should never be able to happen again," she added.'Real worry' for those affectedCredit union trade body Altogether Money receives payment from CMutual for offering products through credit unions.A spokesperson for Altogether Money said the family protection plan had been an optional product that credit unions could choose to offer."The decision as to whether or not to offer such products to credit union members has always been one for individual credit union boards to determine and they are responsible for their regulatory compliance and due diligence in relation to these products," it said."Some have taken decisions to provide financial ex-gratia payments as a goodwill gesture but in doing so are only concerned to support their members as co-operative, member-owned organisations and do not admit any liability."Each credit union should consider its own financial, legal and regulatory position in offering such support and we are providing advice and guidance to credit unions that wish to do so."The Financial Conduct Authority investigated the cancellation of the plan, and acknowledged the closure had caused "real worry" to those affected."We have looked carefully at the circumstances. Based on this evidence, we have decided against taking further action in relation to historical conduct at this time," said a spokesperson."This was a renewable life insurance product, meaning that the insurer was not required to provide it indefinitely – and we don't have the power to make them continue."We know this is disappointing. We have strongly encouraged the firms involved to help impacted consumers and will support them to achieve this."The coalition of credit unions will hold a meeting on Wednesday with the UK Treasury, which previously said it was holding talks with the industry and encouraging those involved to "explore all options" to support those affected.In a statement issued in 2025, Maiden Life said the interests of CMutual's clients and policyholders had been "foremost in our plans" during its dealings with the insurance broker."As part of closing our life business we ensured we gave CMutual considerable notice to enable them to inform and provide their customers with alternative arrangements," it said.A spokesperson for CMutual said the FPP had been "much valued" by credit unions and their members.It said more than 70% of those holding a policy had claimed at least once, and over 25% had claimed more than once. The FPP enabled the policyholder to claim after the death of other people named on the policy.CMutual also said the FCA had concluded that many people aged 80 and under were likely to be able to secure other insurance cover."Credit unions across the United Kingdom have a tremendous record of supporting and safeguarding their members, and we remain instrumental in helping them achieve this," it said."For those members and insureds most affected by the withdrawal of FPP, including those aged over 80 years for whom alternative cover may not be widely available, we remain supportive of both individual credit union initiatives already implemented and sector wide discussions to support such members."

schema.headline: George thought his funeral was paid for – but now his wife will get nothing when he dies

title: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi
description: The spokesperson added that the meeting also touched on the success of the annual Earthshot Prize ceremony, and India's "growing leadership in environ
body: The spokesperson added that the meeting also touched on the success of the annual Earthshot Prize ceremony, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".On Tuesday the prince and princess were in Mumbai to announce the winners of the Earthshot Prize. The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.Five separate winners were named during Tuesday's ceremony and each will receive £1m to scale up their projects.  Speaking at the ceremony, Prince William said the 2020s were the time when positive change becomes "irreversible", adding history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.The princess presented on the five awards and, as she did so, said the entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis brought her "hope". The royal couple's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

schema.headline: William and Kate reflect on 'enduring' UK-India ties with Modi

title: Hacks, AI or overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByImran Rahman-JonesTechnology reporterWhat's been going on?As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByImran Rahman-JonesTechnology reporterWhat's been going on?As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend. Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world. And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out. Why are these happening now?Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models."I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.This happened in the recent Java incident, as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.Then there are the outages.These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt. Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre. How worried should we be?US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker."We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.At the same time, Anthropic, among other leading AI firms, has warned of the risks its own products pose.Outages in particular have an impact on the physical world as they often cause disruption to healthcare, schools and people's ability to do their jobs.Or, in the case over the weekend, planes' ability to fly.Figure caption, Watch: Marco Rubio says recent tech outages are 'completely unrelated' to one anotherThey also shine a light on the world's heavy reliance on a small number of players.Not just frontier AI companies, but infrastructure providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, which - along with Google - run a huge chunk of the world's computer servers.In the PHP incident, the world was holding its breath as one programmer - working voluntarily - worked to issue patches in a form that was easily applicable.And Java, run by another tech giant Oracle, is used by nearly all of the biggest companies on Earth. "The Oracle Java vulnerability is a stark reminder of how dependent businesses have become on a relatively small number of critical technologies," said Sheila Pancholi, risk assurance lead at consultancy firm RSM UK. "Organisations need to know where their critical technology dependencies sit, act quickly when vulnerabilities emerge, and test that their response has actually worked."Meanwhile Xander Van Raemdonck, security engineer at Aikido Security, said the challenge was "knowing whether you're exposed"."Java is bundled inside a huge amount of business software, so many companies don't have a full list of where it runs," he said.Is this the new normal?Perhaps for now. The AI tools used to help find security flaws are still so new that they will probably continue to find vulnerabilities which have been lingering in code for decades."AI is accelerating discovery on both sides and speeding up how much software gets shipped," said Martin Reynolds, field CTO at software delivery company Harness. "So the volume of what developers need to patch is going up, while the time they have to get the work done it is going down."Tech debt will need to continue to be dealt with - which means more upgrades to systems and more potential for these to cause disruptions. Plus there is the constant threat from hackers as they continue to get more sophisticated. Attackers only need to find one vulnerability to exploit - whereas defenders have to protect against all potential hacks."Attackers can move quickly and carefree, and experiment without risk of failure so they can naturally often move a fraction faster," Helme said."We're currently observing that small delay between how fast the attackers can move and how fast the defenders can move."The cat-and-mouse nature of the cyber-security game means it's unlikely to end any time soon - and the impact of AI means the stakes are getting higher.

schema.headline: Hacks, AI or overdue updates - why have there been so many outages?

title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rate rises again
description: Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in
body: Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates. It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".Additional reporting by Raphael Sheridan, economics producer

schema.headline: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as UK inflation rate rises again

title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
description: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela AmodeiByTom EspinerBusiness reporterIn t
body: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Brother and sister Dario and Daniela AmodeiByTom EspinerBusiness reporterIn the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each. If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?Dario AmodeiImage source, Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesIn 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profileDaniela AmodeiImage source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.Tom BrownImage source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesTom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.Jack ClarkImage source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty ImagesJack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.Jared KaplanImage source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesJared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.Chris OlahImage source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty ImagesChris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.Sam McCandlishImage source, AnthropicSam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

schema.headline: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires

title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
description: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Gr
body: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype." But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building. "The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors. Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action. But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics."They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review."It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it."While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m). The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

schema.headline: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
